newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi's Hutu rebels announce 11-day ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's Hutu rebels announce 11-day ceasefire.

text.p: The main Hutu rebel group in Burundi announced a unilateral ceasefire from midnight (2100 GMT) on Monday but said it would hit back against any moves by the army.
Leonard Nyangoma, head of the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) and its armed wing, announced the 11-day ceasefire in a Christmas and New Year's message.
But he warned Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army against trying to attack rebel positions or redeploy troops during the ceasefire, saying the rebels would hit back with full force.

"CNDD...declares a general ceasefire of 11 days from Monday, December 23, 1996, at midnight until Thursday, January 3, 1997, at midnight so the Burundian people can celebrate in happiness and peace Christmas and New Year," Nyangoma said.

"We however warn the bloodthirsty army...against profiting from this ceasefire...to attack our positions or redeploy its forces on the ground. In that case, we will hit back with the greatest energy," Nyangoma added in a written statement.
He accused the army of massacring tens of thousands of defenceless civilians including women and children in 1996 including refugees forced to return to Burundi last month from eastern Zaire.
More than 150,000 people -- most of them civilians -- have been killed in massacres and civil war between the army and Hutu rebels since the assassination of Burundi's first Hutu president in 1993.

Nyangoma said that in less than two years rebel forces controlled most of the country and CNDD was being invited to meetings and talks on the same level as the military junta which seized power on July 25.

It said recently a CNDD delegation had met Julius Nyerere, the former Tanzanian president and now international mediator on Burundi, in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha, at the same time as he met representatives of Burundi's military junta.
"The time is coming when we will reveal other meetings," it said.
Nyangoma responded to diplomats saying the Burundian army gained from a Tutsi-led rebellion in eastern Zaire because it forced rebels out of their bases there and back into Burundi.

"CNDD has sufficient forces to hit the government army in the near future and our forces are growing every day," he said. "We are well installed in the interior of the country and all our operations are launched from bases in the interior."
He denied accusations by Rwanda's military rulers that CNDD was also operating from refugee camps in northwestern Tanzania.
Tanzania has ordered all 540,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees to leave by the end of the year but the deadline does not apply to the 100,000 Burundian refugees also in camps in the northwest.
Nyangoma urged Burundians to heed the advice of its local representatives and produce a surplus to give to the rebels.
Travellers from Buchaganzwa in east Burundi said on Sunday 250 civilians were killed with guns and bayonets in a massacre when the Burundi army attacked Hutu rebels in the area last month.
Officials in Bujumbura said on Sunday that only 19 people had been killed in army operations in the area last month.

The government on Saturday denied a report by London-based Amnesty International that security forces killed at least 1,000 unarmed Hutu civilians in the past month, some while sheltering in churches.
Amnesty said up to 500 people were massacred in a church at Nyarurama on December 3 60 km (40 miles) southeast of Bujumbura.
